dok_rationale: Part (c) coordinates selection method, response count, and target population to choose between competing estimates, explain why sample size cannot repair self-selection, and match a design change to the bias.
stem: Suppose a school website posts the question, ``Should the cafeteria go cashless?'' Any visitor may answer. Of 412 responses, $71\%$ say Yes. That same week, a teacher randomly selects three homerooms and asks every student in those rooms. Of 68 responses, $44\%$ say Yes.\par\smallskip The website headline is ``Students back a cashless cafeteria.'' The teacher's headline is ``Students are split on going cashless.''
first_take: Which headline would you trust more for what students at this school think? Name one detail behind your choice.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Who is the population the headlines are trying to describe?

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: In two sentences, explain how students entered each poll and which students the website poll could miss.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Which percentage is more trustworthy for this school? Explain how selection supports your choice and why the larger response count does not settle it. Suggest one change that directly improves who enters the website sample.

answers.b: Website visitors choose whether to answer; people who do not visit or do not feel strongly may be missed. The teacher selects homerooms by chance and asks everyone in the chosen rooms; the method's formal name is not required today.
answers.c: The $44\%$ result is more trustworthy because the homerooms were selected by chance. The website's 412 responses do not repair self-selection: volunteers may differ from other students. Select students by chance from the full school roster, invite only those selected, and follow up with them instead of accepting an open poll. Three rooms can still differ from the school by chance; this choice does not guarantee the exact school percentage.

expectedElements.description: Chooses 44 percent using chance selection rather than sample size
Explains how website volunteers may differ and why 412 does not remove that problem
Proposes chance selection from the school population instead of open volunteering

scoringGuide.E: All three elements are correct and linked to this problem. Accept equivalent plain-language reasoning.
scoringGuide.P: At least one element includes a correct evidence-to-reason link, but another is missing or incorrect.
scoringGuide.I: No correct evidence-to-reason link; only a choice, copied numbers, or unsupported statements.

commonMistakes: Choosing the larger sample solely because 412 exceeds 68
Calling the website poll random because many different visitors could answer
Saying only that the polls disagree without analyzing who chose to respond
Keeping the poll open to everyone but changing only its wording
